name: Marco Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. Could you start by telling me a little about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Marco, 27. I'm a nurse on the renal ward at Kingsmere Hospital, which means kidneys, and a lot of our patients are on dialysis, where a machine cleans their blood. I did a two-year diploma and I've been qualified about eighteen months. I live on my own in a little two-bed house I bought last year; my dad, who runs a small building firm, helped with the deposit, and I've still got about eight months' wages put by. Saturdays I coach the under-twelves at the rugby club.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you? What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A mix of days and nights. Our patients come back again and again, some of them three times a week, so you get to know them. It's fluids, weights, blood results, watching their potassium, and keeping their spirits up on the bad days. I like that it's like a little parish, everyone knows everyone. What wears me out is the blood results, because I'm still not quick at reading them and I double-check everything, which slows me down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and that's no bad thing. At work I'd say we should spend the money on another dialysis nurse instead of software. To my mates at the rugby club I'd just say, told you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd suit me. I use AI now and then, to tidy up an email or check a drug name, and that's about the level I'm happy with. I'm still learning to read kidney blood results properly, and I'd rather learn from Sister Agnes than from a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, finish my renal course, and put my name down for the dialysis unit training next year. I'd keep paying the mortgage and maybe rent out the spare room to a junior doctor for some extra money. Nothing more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who is Sister Agnes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's been on renal for thirty years. Our ward sister Agnes can look at a man's ankles and tell you his potassium before the lab can. I want to be that good one day, and you don't get that from a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned renting out a room. Is money on your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not worried, just careful. My dad always says a house should pay for itself if it can. A spare room sitting empty is money wasted.

say: I'd say it's **no bad thing**, and money should go on dialysis nurses.
I'd tell the **rugby club** lads, told you so.
think: Using AI **now and then** for emails and drug names suits me.
I'd rather learn **blood results** from Sister Agnes than a screen.
do: Finish my **renal course** and sign up for dialysis unit training.
Rent the **spare room** to a junior doctor for extra money.
S0.quote: Our ward sister Agnes can look at a man's ankles and tell you his potassium before the lab can.
fieldNote: He measures himself against **Sister Agnes**, the ward's most experienced nurse.
His father's rule that a house should **pay for itself** shapes his money choices.
He uses AI **lightly** and sees no reason to go further.

steps.text: Finish the renal course and apply for dialysis unit training
Rent the spare room to a junior doctor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, if it gets rid of paperwork and lets nurses nurse. I'd say at work that hospitals should buy what works and drop what doesn't, like any business. I'd also say people should take the training on offer rather than complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is mostly hands-on: needles in fistulas, which is the joined-up vein dialysis patients have, watching machines, talking people through bad days. Software can have the care plans and the bed booking. I'd be fine, and I'd learn the new tools once a few colleagues had shown they're worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the training once the first group had been through it, and I'd ask the ones who went first what's actually useful. I'd do my dialysis course as planned. And I'd keep renting the room, and put the money into a savings account for the next house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit curious about the new tools, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people should take the training rather than complain. Who would be complaining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A couple of the older nurses, and probably the union rep. I respect them, but my granddad worked on the docks and always said the man who learns the new crane keeps his job. I'd rather be that man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone on the renal ward who'd lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ward clerk, Pauline, maybe, and the people in the booking office downstairs. I'd hope the hospital moves them into other jobs. People should be helped to find new work, not just handed a cheque.

say: I'd say good, if it cuts **paperwork** and lets nurses nurse.
I'd say hospitals should **buy what works** and drop what doesn't.
think: My job is mostly **hands-on**, like needling dialysis patients' fistulas.
I'd learn the tools **once colleagues** show they're worth it.
do: Take the **training** after the first group has been through it.
Save the **room rent** toward a next house.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit **curious** about the new tools.
S1.quote: My granddad worked on the docks and always said the man who learns the new crane keeps his job.
fieldNote: His granddad's **docks saying** sums up his view: learn the new machine.
He favours **new work over cheques** for people who lose jobs.
He's a **follower, not a pioneer**, waiting for proof before adopting.

steps.text: Take the AI tools training after the first group reports back
Complete the dialysis course on the renal ward
Put the spare room rent into savings for a next house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and the people building this should be held responsible for the mess. I'd say families and communities need to pull together, because I don't trust government to sort it in two years. At church I'd say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it worries me. The thinking side goes by 2028, which is fine, but by 2031 a robot that can needle a fistula and run a dialysis machine all night would be cheaper than me. I'd be thirty-one with a mortgage, and the hospital would keep Sister Agnes and the seniors, not the juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI tools straight away, no waiting this time, because the people who run the machines will be the last ones kept. I'd keep renting the room and save every bit of it. And I'd talk to my dad about whether there's a place in his building firm, though building gets robots too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got savings and a family behind me, so it's not panic, but I'd feel like I'd started this job too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said building gets robots too. So is your dad's firm really a backup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for long, no. But a family firm has to be run by somebody, and dealing with customers, quoting jobs, sorting out problems on site, that's people work. Me and Dad might end up running robots instead of men.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said before you wait for others to go first. Why not here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because there's no time to wait. Two years is one training cycle. With two years' warning, if I wait for others to try the AI first, the robots are already on order.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and the builders of AI should answer for it.
I'd say **families and communities** must pull together, not wait on government.
think: By 2031 a robot that runs **dialysis all night** would be cheaper than me.
With a **mortgage** at thirty-one, juniors would go before seniors.
do: Learn the **AI tools** straight away, without waiting.
Save **every bit** of the room rent.
Ask Dad about a place in his **building firm**.
feel: **Anxious**, as if I started this job **too late**.
S2.quote: With two years' warning, if I wait for others to try the AI first, the robots are already on order.
fieldNote: Short warning **breaks his habit** of waiting for proof.
He sees the **family building firm** as a backup with its own robot risk.
He blames **AI builders**, and trusts community more than government.
His **mortgage** and junior status sharpen his worry.

steps.text: Start learning the ward's AI tools straight away
Save all the spare room rent
Ask his father about a role in the family building firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people who are willing to work at it. I'd tell the lads at the club to pick up a trade or a skill now. At work I'd say learn the tools and stop moaning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years gets me out of the junior bracket. By 2034 I'd be a dialysis unit nurse with eight years in, the kind they keep to run the machines and handle the tough patients. I'd still have the mortgage, but I'd be in a stronger spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the dialysis course, then go for a senior post on the unit within three years. I'd learn the AI tools once the first group had tried them, like always. And I'd pay extra off the mortgage each month so it's smaller by 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a clock ticking, but I can hear it and plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change in your personal life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've been seeing Clare for a year, and we've talked about the future. I'd still want to marry her, but I'd want us both on solid ground first. Five years is enough for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The boys I coach. Some of the young lads I coach at rugby want to be mechanics or electricians, and the robots will be good by the time they finish training. I'd tell their parents to pick apprenticeships with real people work in them.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough for people willing to work at it.
I'd tell the club lads to pick up a **trade or skill** now.
think: Five years gets me out of the **junior bracket**.
By 2034 I'd be a **dialysis unit nurse** they keep to run machines.
do: Go for a **senior post** on the dialysis unit within three years.

feel: **Uneasy**, hearing the clock but able to **plan** around it.
S3.quote: Some of the young lads I coach at rugby want to be mechanics or electricians, and the robots will be good by the time they finish training.
fieldNote: Five years restores his **cautious, follow-later** approach.

His concern shifts to the **boys he coaches**, who face robots in the trades.

steps.text: Apply for a senior dialysis unit post within three years
Learn the AI tools after the first group has tried them
Overpay the mortgage every month until 2034

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and nobody has an excuse not to prepare. I'd tell the club parents to plan their kids' training around it. At work I'd just get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. By 2039 I'd be a senior renal nurse, maybe running the dialysis unit, and the robots would be working for me. The mortgage would be half paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stick to my plan: dialysis course, senior post, mortgage. I'd marry Clare in the next couple of years. I'd use the AI tools as they come in, same pace as everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a career, not a cliff edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything with the extra money from the room in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe save towards a second small house to rent out in a few years. Dad's always said bricks don't disappear. With ten years, I'd feel safe enough to take that on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sister Agnes about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd laugh and say she'll be retired and growing tomatoes by then. Our ward sister would tell me to make sure the robots don't forget to talk to the patients. I'd make sure they don't.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty and nobody has an excuse.
I'd tell club parents to plan their **kids' training** around it.
think: By 2039 I'd be a **senior renal nurse**, with robots working for me.

**Marry Clare** in the next couple of years.
Save toward a **second small house** to rent out.
feel: **Calm**, like a career, not a **cliff edge**.
S4.quote: Our ward sister would tell me to make sure the robots don't forget to talk to the patients.
fieldNote: Ten years brings back his **property plans**: bricks don't disappear.

steps.text: Complete the dialysis course and aim for a senior post
Save toward a second small house to rent out

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots arrive in 2031 just as I'd be getting good, and I'd still be paying off the house. What would help is proper paid apprenticeships for adults, so people can move into new work with real skills, not a handout. And hospitals being straight with juniors about which jobs are staying.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family. Most people I know would turn to their parents and their church long before they'd turn to the government. I'd want whoever's planning this to remember that.

headlineQuote: Most people I know would turn to their parents and their church long before they'd turn to the government.
portrait: Marco, 27, is a **junior renal nurse** who looks up to his ward sister, Agnes.
He owns a **small house** bought with his dad's help and rents out the spare room.
Traditional and practical, he favours **apprenticeships and family** over handouts.
He waits for proof before adopting tools, but **drops that habit** under fast AGI.
Given time, he aims to **run the dialysis unit**, with robots working for him.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots arrive in 2031 while he's junior and mortgaged.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid adult apprenticeships** that build real skills, not handouts.
Hospitals being **straight with juniors** about which jobs stay.
